chunks: I was in the gathering of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) when Amr ibn Ubayd entered upon him
and said to him: 'May I be your ransom! Concerning the Word of God, Blessed and Exalted: "and whosoever My wrath befalls, he has indeed perished" [20:81] — what is that wrath?'

So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'It is the punishment, O Amr. Indeed, whoever claims that God has transitioned from one state to another has described Him with an attribute of a creature, and God the Exalted — nothing stirs Him so that He would change.'

key_terms.الْعِقَابُ: The punishment — God's wrath as its effectual consequence, not an inner emotional state
key_terms.الْغَضَبُ: The wrath/anger — interpreted here as 'al-iqab' (punishment), not an emotional state
key_terms.زَالَ مِنْ شَيْءٍ إِلَى شَيْءٍ: Transitioned from one thing/state to another — describes change in being, which is a characteristic of creatures
key_terms.صِفَةَ مَخْلُوقٍ: Attribute of a creature — anthropomorphic attribution forbidden of God
key_terms.يَسْتَفِزُّهُ: To stir/agitate — the impossibility of anything disturbing God's eternal unchanging nature

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir teach about the meaning of God's wrath (ghadab) in the Quran?
ai.summary: An anonymous companion narrates that Amr ibn Ubayd, a Mu'tazilite theologian known for his emphasis on divine anthropomorphism critiques, posed a question to Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (peace be upon him) about the Quranic phrase 'My wrath' in Surah Ta-Ha. The Imam's response is a foundational Shia theological statement: God's 'wrath' is not an emotional state but rather the resulting punishment — and to attribute to God a transition between states (like from calm to angry) is to describe Him with the attributes of creatures. This teaching affirms divine immutability (that God does not undergo change or emotional fluctuation) and is a key hadith in Shia kalaam literature distinguishing divine attributes of essence from attributes of action.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Al Barqy, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Al Mashraqy Hamza Bin Al Mutafa’a, from one of our companions who said, 
‘I was in a gathering of Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> when Amro Bin Ubeyd came over to him<sup>asws</sup>
and said to himasws, ‘May I be sacrificed for youasws! The Words of Allahazwj Blessed and High [20:81], and whomsoever My Anger is due upon so he has perished. What is that Anger?’

So Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘It is the Punishment, O Amro, and he who alleges that Allah<sup>azwj</sup> has ceased to be from a thing to a thing, so he has described Him<sup>azwj</sup> with an attribute of a creature, and that Allah<sup>azwj</sup> the Exalted. Nothing stirs Him<sup>azwj</sup>, so He<sup>azwj</sup> would change’.
en.sarwar: 5. A group of our people has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi from Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from al-Mashriqi Hamzah ibn al-Murtafi‘ from some of our people who has said the following. “I was in the presence of abu Ja‘far (a.s.) when ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd said, ‘May Allah take my soul in your service,
what is the meaning of Allah’s words, “Whoever becomes subject to my anger he is destroyed.” 20:84 What is this anger?’

Abu Ja‘far (a.s.) replied, “O ‘Amr, His anger is His punishment. O ‘Amr, whoever thinks Allah changes from one state to another, has ascribed to Allah the attributes of His creatures. Nothing can provoke Allah, the Sublime, to change Him.”
